{{short description|Probability distribution on a hyper-sphere of arbitrary dimension}}
{{lowercase title}}
In [[directional statistics]], the '''von Mises–Fisher distribution''' (named after [[Richard von Mises]] and [[Ronald Fisher]]), is a [[probability distribution]] on the <math>(p-1)</math>-[[n-sphere|sphere]] in <math>\mathbb{R}^{p}</math>. If <math>p=2</math>
the distribution reduces to the [[von Mises distribution]] on the [[circle]].

== Definition ==
The [[probability density]] function of the von Mises–Fisher distribution for the random ''p''-dimensional unit vector <math>\mathbf{x}</math> is given by:
<math display=block>f_{p}(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu}, \kappa) = C_{p}(\kappa) \exp \left( {\kappa \boldsymbol{\mu}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{x} } \right),</math>
where <math>\kappa \ge 0, \left \Vert \boldsymbol{\mu} \right \Vert = 1</math> and  
the normalization constant <math>C_{p}(\kappa)</math> is equal to
<math display=block>C_{p}(\kappa)=\frac {\kappa^{p/2-1}} {(2\pi)^{p/2}I_{p/2-1}(\kappa)},</math>
where <math>I_{v}</math> denotes the modified [[Bessel function]] of the first kind at order <math>v</math>. If <math>p = 3</math>, the normalization constant reduces to
<math display=block>C_{3}(\kappa) = \frac {\kappa} {4\pi\sinh \kappa} = \frac {\kappa} {2\pi(e^{\kappa}-e^{-\kappa})}.</math>

The parameters <math>\boldsymbol{\mu}</math> and <math>\kappa</math> are called the ''mean direction'' and ''[[concentration parameter]]'', respectively. The greater the value of <math>\kappa</math>, the higher the concentration of the distribution around the mean direction <math>\boldsymbol{\mu}</math>. The distribution is [[unimodal]] for <math>\kappa > 0</math>, and is uniform on the sphere for <math>\kappa = 0</math>.

The von Mises–Fisher distribution for <math>p=3</math> is also called the '''Fisher distribution'''.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Fisher | first1 = R. A. | doi = 10.1098/rspa.1953.0064 | title = Dispersion on a sphere | journal = Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A | volume = 217 | pages = 295–305 | year = 1953| issue = 1130 | bibcode = 1953RSPSA.217..295F | s2cid = 123166853 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Watson | first1 = G. S. | doi = 10.2307/3213566 | title = Distributions on the Circle and on the Sphere | journal = J. Appl. Probab. | volume = 19 | pages = 265–280 | year = 1980| jstor = 3213566 | s2cid = 222325569 }}</ref>
It was first used to model the interaction of [[electric dipole]]s in an [[electric field]].<ref name="MardiaJupp">{{cite book |title=Directional Statistics |last1=Mardia |first1=Kanti |author-link=Kantilal Mardia |last2 = Jupp | first2 = P. E.|year=1999 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons Ltd. |isbn=978-0-471-95333-3}}</ref> Other applications are found in [[geology]], [[bioinformatics]], and [[text mining]].

=== Support ===
The [[support (mathematics)|support]] of the von Mises–Fisher distribution is the ''hypersphere'', or more specifically, the [[n-sphere|<math>(p-1)</math>-sphere]], denoted as 
<math display=block>
\mathbb S^{p-1} = \left\{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^p : \left\| \mathbf{x} \right\| = 1 \right\}
</math>
This is a <math>(p-1)</math>-dimensional [[manifold (mathematics)|manifold]] embedded in <math>p</math>-dimensional Euclidean space, <math>\mathbb{R}^p</math>.

=== Note on the normalization constant ===
In the textbook, ''Directional Statistics'' <ref name="MardiaJupp" /> by [[Kantilal Mardia|Mardia]] and Jupp, the normalization constant given for the von Mises Fisher (VMF) probability density is apparently different from the one given here: <math>C_{p}(\kappa)</math>. In that book, for <math>\text{VMF}(\boldsymbol\mu,\kappa)</math> the normalization constant is specified as:
<math display=block>C^*_{p}(\kappa)=\frac {(\frac{\kappa}2)^{p/2-1}} {\Gamma(p/2)I_{p/2-1}(\kappa)}</math>
where <math>\Gamma</math> is the [[gamma function]]. This is resolved by noting that Mardia and Jupp give the density "with respect to the uniform distribution", while the density here is specified with respect to  [[Hausdorff_measure#Scaled_Hausdorff_measure|scaled Hausdorff measure]], <math>\bar H^{p-1}</math>, which gives [[n-sphere#Volume and surface area|the surface area of the whole ''(p-1)''-sphere]] as:
<math display=block>
H^{p-1}_\lambda(\mathbb S^{p-1}) = \frac{2\pi^{p/2}}{\Gamma(p/2)},
</math>
the reciprocal of which gives the (constant) density of the uniform distribution, <math>\text{VMF}(\boldsymbol\mu,\kappa=0),</math> as:
<math display=block>C_{p}(0)=\frac{\Gamma(p/2)}{2\pi^{p/2}}</math>
It then follows that:
<math display=block>C^*_{p}(\kappa) = \frac{C_{p}(\kappa)}{C_{p}(0)}</math>
While the value for <math>C_{p}(0)</math> was derived above via the surface area, the same result may be obtained by setting <math>\kappa=0</math> in the above formula for <math>C_{p}(\kappa)</math>. This can be done by noting that the [[Bessel function#Modified Bessel functions: Iα, Kα|series expansion for <math>I_{p/2-1}(\kappa)</math>]] divided by <math>\kappa^{p/2-1}</math> has but one non-zero term at <math>\kappa=0</math>. (To evaluate that term, one needs to use the [[Zero to the power of zero|definition]] <math>0^0=1</math>.)

For further understanding of density functions on the hypersphere, see: {{slink|projected normal distribution|note on density definition}}.

== Relation to normal distribution ==

Starting from a [[multivariate normal distribution]] with [[isotropic]] [[covariance]] <math>\kappa^{-1}\mathbf{I}</math> and mean <math>\boldsymbol{\mu}</math> of length <math>r>0</math>, whose density function is: 
<math display=block>\mathcal N_{p}(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu}, \kappa)
= \left(\sqrt{\frac{\kappa}{2\pi}}\right)^p \exp\left( -\kappa \frac{(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\mathsf{T}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})}{2} \right),</math>
the von Mises–Fisher distribution is obtained by conditioning on <math>\left\|\mathbf{x}\right\|=1</math>. By expanding
<math display=block>(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\mathsf{T}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}) = \mathbf{x}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{x} + \boldsymbol{\mu}^\mathsf{T}\boldsymbol{\mu} - 2\boldsymbol{\mu}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{x}=1+r^2-2\boldsymbol\mu^\mathsf{T}\mathbf x,
</math>
the von Mises–Fisher density, <math>f_{p}(\mathbf{x}; r^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}, r\kappa)\propto e^{\kappa\boldsymbol{\mu}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{x}}</math> is recovered by recomputing the normalization constant by integrating <math>\mathbf{x}</math> over the unit sphere. If <math>\boldsymbol\mu=\boldsymbol0</math>, we get the uniform distribution, with (constant) density <math>f_{p}(\mathbf{x}; \tilde\boldsymbol\mu, 0)</math>, where <math>\tilde\boldsymbol\mu\in\mathbb S^{p-1}</math> is arbitrary.

More succinctly, the [[restriction (mathematics)|restriction]] of any isotropic multivariate normal density to the unit hypersphere gives a von Mises–Fisher density, up to normalization.

See also:
* This construction can be generalized by starting with a normal distribution with a general covariance matrix, in which case restricting to <math>\left\|\mathbf{x}\right\|=1</math> gives the [[Fisher-Bingham distribution]].
* Restriction is not to be confused with [[Projection_(mathematics)|projection]]. If <math>\mathbf z\sim\mathcal N_p(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\Sigma)</math>, which we project onto the unitsphere: <math>\mathbf x=\lVert\mathbf z\rVert^{-1}\mathbf z</math>, we get the [[projected normal distribution]]. (Informally, restriction can be thought of as [[rejection sampling]] with an infinite sampling budget, where we keep only those <math>\mathbf z</math> that land on the unitsphere, while with projection we use all samples.)

== Estimation of parameters ==

=== Mean direction ===
A series of ''N'' [[independence (probability theory)|independent]] [[unit vector]]s <math>x_i</math> are drawn from a von Mises–Fisher distribution. 
The [[maximum likelihood]] estimates of the mean direction <math>\mu</math> is simply the normalized [[arithmetic mean]], a [[sufficient statistic]]:<ref name="MardiaJupp"/>
<math display=block>\mu = \bar{x}/\bar{R},
\text{where }
\bar{x} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i^N x_i,
\text{and }
\bar{R} = \|\bar{x}\|,</math>

=== Concentration parameter ===
Use the modified [[Bessel function of the first kind]] to define
<math display=block>A_{p}(\kappa) = \frac {I_{p/2}(\kappa)} {I_{p/2-1}(\kappa)}\,.</math>

Then:
<math display=block>\kappa = A_p^{-1}(\bar{R})\,.</math>
Thus <math>\kappa</math> is the solution to
<math display=block>A_p(\kappa) = \frac{\left\| \sum_i^N x_i \right\|}{N} = \bar{R}\,.</math>

A simple approximation to <math>\kappa</math> is (Sra, 2011)
<math display=block>\hat{\kappa} = \frac{\bar{R}(p-\bar{R}^2)}{1-\bar{R}^2}\,,</math>

A more accurate inversion can be obtained by iterating the [[Newton method]] a few times
<math display=block>\hat{\kappa}_1 = \hat{\kappa} - \frac{A_p(\hat{\kappa}) - \bar{R}}{1-A_p(\hat{\kappa})^2 - \frac{p - 1}{\hat{\kappa}} A_p(\hat{\kappa})}\,,</math>
<math display=block>\hat{\kappa}_2 = \hat{\kappa}_1 - \frac{A_p(\hat{\kappa}_1)-\bar{R}}{1-A_p(\hat{\kappa}_1)^2-\frac{p - 1}{\hat{\kappa}_1} A_p(\hat{\kappa}_1)}\,.</math>

=== Standard error ===
For ''N''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;25, the estimated spherical [[standard error]] of the sample mean direction can be computed as:<ref>{{cite book|last=Embleton|first=N. I. Fisher, T. Lewis, B. J. J.|title=Statistical analysis of spherical data|year=1993|publisher=Cambridge University Press|location=Cambridge|isbn=0-521-45699-1|pages=[https://archive.org/details/statisticalanaly0000fish/page/115 115–116]|edition=1st pbk.|url=https://archive.org/details/statisticalanaly0000fish/page/115}}</ref> 
<math display=block>\hat{\sigma} = \left(\frac{d}{N\bar{R}^2}\right)^{1/2}</math>
where
<math display=block>d = 1 - \frac{1}{N} \sum_i^N \left(\mu^Tx_i\right)^2</math>
It is then possible to approximate a <math>100(1-\alpha)\%</math> a spherical [[confidence interval]] (a ''confidence cone'') about <math>\mu</math> with semi-vertical angle:
<math display=block>q = \arcsin\left(e_\alpha^{1/2}\hat{\sigma}\right),</math> where <math>e_\alpha = -\ln(\alpha).</math>
For example, for a 95% confidence cone, <math>\alpha = 0.05, e_\alpha = -\ln(0.05) = 2.996,</math> and thus <math>q = \arcsin(1.731\hat{\sigma}).</math>

== Expected value ==
The expected value of the von Mises–Fisher distribution is not on the unit hypersphere, but instead has a length of less than one. This length is given by <math>A_p(\kappa)</math> as defined above. For a von Mises–Fisher distribution with mean direction <math>\boldsymbol{\mu}</math> and concentration <math>\kappa>0</math>, the expected value is: 
<math display=block>A_p(\kappa)\boldsymbol{\mu}</math>. 
For <math>\kappa=0</math>, the expected value is at the origin. For finite <math>\kappa>0</math>, the length of the expected value is strictly between zero and one and is a monotonic rising function of <math>\kappa</math>.

The empirical mean ([[arithmetic average]]) of a collection of points on the unit hypersphere behaves in a similar manner, being close to the origin for widely  spread data and close to the sphere for concentrated data. Indeed, for the von Mises–Fisher distribution, the expected value of the maximum-likelihood estimate based on a collection of points is equal to the empirical mean of those points.

== Entropy and KL divergence ==
The expected value can be used to compute [[differential entropy]] and [[KL divergence]].

The '''differential entropy''' of <math>\text{VMF}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \kappa)</math> is:
<math display=block>
\bigl\langle -\log f_{p}(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu}, \kappa)\bigr\rangle_{\mathbf{x}\sim\text{VMF}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \kappa)}
=-\log f_{p}(A_p(\kappa)\boldsymbol{\mu}; \boldsymbol{\mu}, \kappa)
= -\log C_p(\kappa) -\kappa A_p(\kappa) 
</math>
where the angle brackets denote expectation. Notice that the entropy is a function of <math>\kappa</math> only.

The '''KL divergence''' between <math>\text{VMF}(\boldsymbol{\mu_0}, \kappa_0)</math> and <math>\text{VMF}(\boldsymbol{\mu_1}, \kappa_1)</math> is:
<math display=block>
\Bigl\langle \log \frac{f_{p}(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu_0}, \kappa_0)}
{f_{p}(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\mu_1}, \kappa_1)}
\Bigr\rangle_{\mathbf{x}\sim\text{VMF}(\boldsymbol{\mu_0}, \kappa_0)}
=\log \frac{f_{p}(A_p(\kappa_0)\boldsymbol{\mu_0}; \boldsymbol{\mu_0}, \kappa_0)}
{f_{p}(A_p(\kappa_0)\boldsymbol{\mu_0}; \boldsymbol{\mu_1}, \kappa_1)}
</math>

== Transformation ==
Von Mises–Fisher (VMF) distributions are closed under orthogonal linear transforms. Let <math>\mathbf{U}</math> be a <math>p</math>-by-<math>p</math> [[orthogonal matrix]]. Let <math>\mathbf{x}\sim\text{VMF}(\boldsymbol\mu,\kappa)</math> and apply the invertible linear transform: <math>\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{Ux}</math>. The inverse transform is <math>\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{U'y}</math>, because the inverse of an orthogonal matrix is its [[transpose]]: <math>\mathbf{U}^{-1}=\mathbf{U}'</math>. The [[Jacobian matrix and determinant|Jacobian]] of the transform is <math>\mathbf{U}</math>, for which the absolute value of its [[determinant]] is 1, also because of the orthogonality. Using these facts and the form of the VMF density, it follows that:  
<math display=block>\mathbf{y}\sim\text{VMF}(\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\mu},\kappa).
</math>
One may verify that since <math>\boldsymbol{\mu}</math> and <math>\mathbf{x}</math> are unit vectors, then by the orthogonality, so are <math>\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\mu}</math> and <math>\mathbf{y}</math>.

== Pseudo-random number generation ==

=== General case ===
An algorithm for drawing pseudo-random samples from the von Mises Fisher (VMF) distribution was given by Ulrich<ref name="Ulrich84" /> and later corrected by Wood.<ref name="Wood94">{{cite journal |last1=Wood |first1=Andrew T |title=Simulation of the Von Mises Fisher distribution |journal=Communications in Statistics - Simulation and Computation |date=1994 |volume=23 |issue=1 |pages=157–164 |doi=10.1080/03610919408813161 |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/03610919408813161|url-access=subscription }}</ref> An implementation in [[R programming language|R]] is given by Hornik and Grün;<ref name="HornikGrun">{{cite journal |last1=Hornik |first1=Kurt |last2=Grün |first2=Bettina |title=movMF: An R Package for Fitting Mixtures of Von Mises–Fisher Distributions |journal=Journal of Statistical Software |date=2014 |volume=58 |issue=10 |doi=10.18637/jss.v058.i10 |s2cid=13171102 |url=https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v058i10|doi-access=free }}</ref> and a fast [[Python programming language|Python]] implementation is described by Pinzón and Jung.<ref  name="PinzonJung">{{Citation |last1=Pinzón |first1=Carlos |title=Fast Python sampler for the von Mises Fisher distribution |date=2023-03-03 |url=https://hal.science/hal-04004568 |access-date=2023-03-30 |language=en |last2=Jung |first2=Kangsoo}}</ref>

To simulate from a VMF distribution on the <math>(p-1)</math>-dimensional [[n-sphere|unitsphere]], <math>S^{p-1}</math>, with mean direction <math>\boldsymbol{\mu}\in S^{p-1}</math>, these algorithms use the following '''radial-tangential decomposition''' for a point <math>\mathbf{x}\in S^{p-1}\subset\mathbb{R}^p</math> :
<math display=block>
\mathbf{x} = t\boldsymbol{\mu}+\sqrt{1-t^2}\mathbf{v}
</math>
where <math>\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^p</math> lives in the tangential <math>(p-2)</math>-dimensional unit-subsphere that is centered at and perpendicular to <math>\boldsymbol{\mu}</math>; while <math>t\in[-1,1]</math>. To draw a sample <math>\mathbf{x}</math> from a VMF with parameters 
<math>\boldsymbol{\mu}</math> and <math>\kappa</math>, <math>\mathbf{v}</math> must be drawn from the uniform distribution on the tangential subsphere; and the radial component, <math>t</math>, must be drawn independently from the distribution with density:
<math display=block>
f_\text{radial}(t;\kappa,p)=\frac{(\kappa/2)^\nu}
{\Gamma(\frac12)\Gamma(\nu+\frac12)I_\nu(\kappa)}
e^{t\kappa}(1-t^2)^{\nu-\frac12}
</math>
where <math>\nu=\frac{p}2-1</math>. The normalization constant for this density may be verified by using:
<math display=block>
I_\nu(\kappa) = \frac{(\kappa/2)^\nu}{\Gamma(\frac12)\Gamma(\nu+\frac12)}
\int_{-1}^{1}e^{t\kappa}(1-t^2)^{\nu-\frac12}\,dt
</math>
as given in Appendix 1 (A.3) in ''Directional Statistics''.<ref name='MardiaJupp'/> Drawing the <math>t</math> samples from this density by using a [[rejection sampling]] algorithm is explained in the above references. To draw the uniform <math>\mathbf{v}</math> samples perpendicular to <math>\boldsymbol{\mu}</math>, see the algorithm in,<ref name = "PinzonJung"/> or otherwise a [[Householder transform]] can be used as explained in Algorithm 1 in.<ref name="DeCaoWilker">{{cite arXiv |last1=De Cao |first1=Nicola |last2=Aziz |first2=Wilker |title=The Power Spherical distribution |date=13 Feb 2023 |class=stat.ML |eprint=2006.04437}}</ref>

=== 3-D sphere ===
To generate a von Mises–Fisher distributed pseudo-random spherical 3-D unit vector<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pakyuz-Charrier |first1=Evren |last2=Lindsay |first2=Mark |last3=Ogarko |first3=Vitaliy |last4=Giraud |first4=Jeremie |last5=Jessell |first5=Mark |date=2018-04-06 |title=Monte Carlo simulation for uncertainty estimation on structural data in implicit 3-D geological modeling, a guide for disturbance distribution selection and parameterization |url=https://se.copernicus.org/articles/9/385/2018/ |journal=Solid Earth |language=English |volume=9 |issue=2 |pages=385–402 |doi=10.5194/se-9-385-2018 |bibcode=2018SolE....9..385P |issn=1869-9510 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=A. |first=Wood, Andrew T. |title=Simulation of the Von Mises Fisher distribution |date=1992 |publisher=Centre for Mathematics & its Applications, Australian National University |oclc=221030477}}</ref> <math display="inline">\mathbf X_{s}</math> on the <math display="inline">S^{2}</math>[[N-sphere|sphere]] for a given <math display="inline">\mu</math> and <math display="inline">\kappa</math>, define
<math display=block>\mathbf X_{s} = [r, \theta, \phi]</math>
where <math display="inline">\theta</math> is the polar angle, <math display="inline">\phi</math> the azimuthal angle, and <math display="inline">r=1</math> the distance to the center of the sphere.

For <math display="inline">\mathbf \mu = [0,(.),1]</math> the pseudo-random triplet is then given by
<math display=block>\mathbf X_{s} = [1, \arccos W, V]</math>
where <math display="inline">V</math> is sampled from the [[continuous uniform distribution]] <math display="inline">U(a,b)</math> with lower bound <math display="inline">a</math> and upper bound <math display="inline">b</math>
<math display=block>V \sim U(0, 2\pi)</math>
and
<math display=block>W = \cos \theta = 1+ \frac {1} {\kappa} (\ln\xi+\ln(1- \frac {\xi-1} {\xi}e^{-2\kappa}))</math>
where <math display="inline">\xi</math> is sampled from the standard continuous uniform distribution <math display="inline">U(0,1)</math>
<math display=block>\xi \sim U(0, 1)</math>
Here, <math display="inline">W</math> should be set to <math display="inline">W = 1</math> when <math display="inline">\mathbf \xi=0</math> and <math display="inline">\mathbf X_{s}</math> rotated to match any other desired <math display="inline">\mu</math>.

== Distribution of polar angle ==

For <math>p = 3</math>, the angle &theta; between <math>\mathbf{x}</math> and <math>\boldsymbol{\mu}</math> satisfies <math>\cos\theta=\boldsymbol{\mu}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{x}</math>. It has the distribution
<math display=block>p(\theta)=\int d^2x f(x; \boldsymbol{\mu}, \kappa)\, \delta\left(\theta-\text{arc cos}(\boldsymbol{\mu}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{x})\right)</math>,
which can be easily evaluated as
<math display=block>p(\theta)=2\pi C_3(\kappa)\,\sin\theta\, e^{\kappa\cos\theta}</math>.

For the general case, <math>p\ge2</math>, the distribution for the cosine of this angle:
<math display=block>
\cos\theta = t = \boldsymbol{\mu}^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{x}
</math>
is given by <math>f_\text{radial}(t;\kappa,p)</math>, as explained [[von Mises–Fisher distribution#Pseudo-random number generation|above]].

== Uniform hypersphere distribution ==
{{See also|N-sphere#Uniformly at random on the (n − 1)-sphere}}

When <math>\kappa=0</math>, the von Mises–Fisher distribution, <math>\text{VMF}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\kappa)</math> simplifies to the '''uniform distribution''' on <math>\mathbb S^{p-1}\subset\mathbb{R}^p</math>. The density is constant with value <math>C_p(0)</math>. Pseudo-random samples can be generated by generating samples in <math>\mathbb{R}^p</math> from the standard multivariate normal distribution, followed by normalization to unit norm.

=== Component marginal of uniform distribution ===
For <math>1\le i\le p</math>, let <math>x_i</math> be any component of <math>\mathbf{x}\in \mathbb S^{p-1}</math>. The '''marginal distribution''' for <math>x_i</math> has the density:<ref name="GosmannEliasmith16">{{cite journal |last1=Gosmann |first1=J |last2=Eliasmith |first2=C |title=Optimizing Semantic Pointer Representations for Symbol-Like Processing in Spiking Neural Networks |journal=PLOS ONE |date=2016 |volume=11 |issue=2 |article-number=e0149928 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0149928 |pmid=26900931 |pmc=4762696 |bibcode=2016PLoSO..1149928G |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Voelker17">{{cite web |last1=Voelker |first1=Aaron R. |last2=Gosmann |first2=Jan |last3=Stewart |first3=Terrence C. |title=Efficiently sampling vectors and coordinates from the n-sphere and n-ball |url=http://compneuro.uwaterloo.ca/files/publications/voelker.2017.pdf |publisher=Centre for Theoretical Neuroscience – Technical Report, 2017 |access-date=22 April 2023}}</ref>
<math display=block>
f_i(x_i;p) = f_\text{radial}(x_i;\kappa=0,p)=\frac{(1-x_i^2)^{\frac{p-1}2-1}}{B\bigl(\frac12,\frac{p-1}2\bigr)}
</math>
where <math>B(\alpha,\beta)</math> is the [[beta function]]. This distribution may be better understood by highlighting its relation to the [[beta distribution]]:
<math display=block>
\begin{align}
x_i^2&\sim\text{Beta}\bigl(\frac12,\frac{p-1}2\bigr) &&\text{and}& 
\frac{x_i+1}{2}&\sim\text{Beta}\bigl(\frac{p-1}2,\frac{p-1}2\bigr)  
\end{align}
</math>
where the [[Multiplication theorem#Gamma function–Legendre formula|Legendre duplication formula]] is useful to understand the relationships between the normalization constants of the various densities above.

Note that the components of <math>\mathbf{x}\in \mathbb S^{p-1}</math> are ''not'' independent, so that the uniform density is not the product of the marginal densities; and <math>\mathbf{x}</math> cannot be assembled by independent sampling of the components.

=== Distribution of dot-products ===
In [[machine learning]], especially in [[image classification]], to-be-classified inputs (e.g. images) are often compared using [[cosine similarity]], which is the [[dot product]] between intermediate representations in the form of unitvectors (termed ''embeddings''). The dimensionality is typically high, with <math>p</math> at least several hundreds. The [[deep neural network]]s that extract embeddings for classification should learn to spread the classes as far apart as possible and ideally this should give classes that are uniformly distributed on <math>\mathbb S^{p-1}</math>.<ref name="Isola202">{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Tongzhou |last2=Isola |first2=Phillip |title=Understanding Contrastive Representation Learning through Alignment and Uniformity on the Hypersphere |journal=International Conference on Machine Learning|date=2020 |arxiv=2005.10242 }}</ref> For a better statistical understanding of ''across-class cosine similarity'', the distribution of dot-products between unitvectors independently sampled from the uniform distribution may be helpful.
 
Let <math>\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in \mathbb S^{p-1}</math> be unitvectors in <math>\mathbb{R}^p</math>, independently sampled from the uniform distribution. Define:
<math display=block>
\begin{align}
t&=\mathbf{x}'\mathbf{y}\in[-1,1], &
r&=\frac{t+1}{2}\in[0,1], &
s&=\text{logit}(r) =\log\frac{1+t}{1-t} \in\mathbb{R}
\end{align}
</math>
where <math>t</math> is the dot-product and <math>r,s</math> are transformed versions of it. Then the distribution for <math>t</math> is the same as the ''marginal component distribution'' given [[von Mises–Fisher distribution#Component marginal of uniform distribution|above]];<ref name="Voelker17"/> the distribution for <math>r</math> is symmetric beta and the distribution for <math>s</math> is  symmetric [[logistic-beta distribution|logistic-beta]]:
<math display=block>
\begin{align}
r&\sim \text{Beta}\bigl(\frac{p-1}2,\frac{p-1}2\bigr), &
s&\sim B_\sigma\bigl(\frac{p-1}2,\frac{p-1}2\bigr)
\end{align}
</math> 
The means and variances are:
<math display=block>
\begin{align}
E[t]&=0, & E[r]&=\frac12, & E[s]&=0,
\end{align}
</math>
and
<math display=block>
\begin{align}
\text{var}[t]&=\frac1p, & \text{var}[r]&=\frac1{4p}, &
\text{var}[s]&=2\psi'\bigl(\frac{p-1}2\bigr)\approx\frac4{p-1}
\end{align}
</math>
where <math>\psi'=\psi^{(1)}</math> is the first [[polygamma function]]. The variances decrease, the distributions of all three variables become more Gaussian, and the final [[Polygamma function#Trigamma bounds and asymptote|approximation]] gets better as the dimensionality, <math>p</math>, is increased.

== Generalizations ==

=== Matrix von Mises–Fisher ===
{{further|Random matrix}}

The '''matrix von Mises–Fisher distribution''' (also known as '''matrix Langevin distribution'''<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chikuse |first1=Yasuko |title=Concentrated matrix Langevin distributions |journal=Journal of Multivariate Analysis |date=1 May 2003 |volume=85 |issue=2 |pages=375–394 |doi=10.1016/S0047-259X(02)00065-9 |language=en |issn=0047-259X|doi-access=free }}</ref>) has the density
<math display=block>f_{n, p}(\mathbf{X}; \mathbf{F}) \propto \exp(\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{F}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{X}))</math>
supported on the [[Stiefel manifold]] of <math>n \times p</math> [[orthonormal]] [[k-frame|p-frames]] <math>\mathbf{X}</math>, where <math>\mathbf{F}</math> is an arbitrary <math>n \times p</math> real matrix.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Jupp | year = 1979 | title = Maximum likelihood estimators for the matrix von Mises–Fisher and Bingham distributions | url = https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.aos/1176344681 | journal = The Annals of Statistics | volume = 7 | issue = 3 | pages = 599–606 | doi = 10.1214/aos/1176344681 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Downs | year = 1972 | title = Orientational statistics | journal = Biometrika | volume = 59 | issue = 3 | pages = 665–676 | doi=10.1093/biomet/59.3.665}}</ref>

=== Saw distributions ===
Ulrich,<ref name="Ulrich84">{{cite journal |last1=Ulrich |first1=Gary |title=Computer generation of distributions on the m-sphere |journal=Applied Statistics |date=1984 |volume=33 |issue=2 |pages=158–163 |doi=10.2307/2347441 |jstor=2347441 }}</ref> in designing an algorithm for sampling from the VMF distribution, makes use of a family of distributions named after and explored by John G. Saw.<ref name="Saw78">{{cite journal |last1=Saw |first1=John G |title=A family of distributions on the m-sphere and some hypothesis tests |journal=Biometrika |date=1978 |volume=65 |issue=` |pages=69–73 |doi=10.2307/2335278 |jstor=2335278 }}</ref> A '''Saw distribution''' is a distribution on the <math>(p-1)</math>-sphere, <math>S^{p-1}</math>, with modal vector <math>\boldsymbol{\mu}\in S^{p-1}</math> and concentration <math>\kappa\ge0</math>, and of which the density function has the form:
<math display=block>
f_\text{Saw}(\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\mu,\kappa)
= \frac{g(\kappa\mathbf x'\boldsymbol\mu)}{K_p(\kappa)}
</math> 
where <math>g</math> is a non-negative, increasing function; and where <math>K_P(\kappa)</math> is the normalization constant. The [[von Mises–Fisher distribution#Pseudo-random number generation|above-mentioned]] ''radial-tangential decomposition'' generalizes to the Saw family and the radial component, <math>t=\mathbf x'\boldsymbol\mu</math> has the density:
<math display=block>
f_\text{Saw-radial}(t;\kappa)=\frac{2\pi^{p/2}}{\Gamma(p/2)}\frac{g(\kappa t)(1-t^2)^{(p-3)/2}}{B\bigl(\frac12,\frac{p-1}2\bigr)K_p(\kappa)}.
</math>
where <math>B</math> is the beta function. Also notice that the left-hand factor of the radial density is the surface area of <math>S^{p-1}</math>.

By setting <math>g(\kappa\mathbf x'\boldsymbol\mu)=e^{\kappa\mathbf x'\boldsymbol\mu}</math>, one recovers the VMF distribution.

=== Weighted Rademacher distribution ===
The definition of the von Mises–Fisher distribution can be extended to include also the case where <math>p=1</math>, so that the support is the 0-dimensional hypersphere, which when embedded into 1-dimensional Euclidean space is the discrete set, <math>\{-1,1\}</math>. The mean direction is <math>\mu\in\{-1,1\}</math> and the concentration is <math>\kappa\ge0</math>. The probability mass function, for <math>x\in\{-1,1\}</math> is:
<math display=block>
f_1(x\mid\mu,\kappa) = \frac{e^{\kappa\mu x}}{e^{-\kappa}+e^{\kappa}}
= \sigma(2\kappa\mu x)
</math>
where <math>\sigma(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})</math> is the [[logistic sigmoid]]. The expected value is <math>\mu\,\text{tanh}(\kappa)</math>. In the uniform case, at <math>\kappa=0</math>, this distribution degenerates to the [[Rademacher distribution]].
